blocks.text: Definition: Two non-zero vectors \(\underline{u}\) and \(\underline{v}\) are perpendicular if and only if \(\underline{u} \cdot \underline{v} = 0\).

Since angle between \(\underline{u}\) and \(\underline{v}\) is \(\frac{\pi}{2}\) and \(\cos\frac{\pi}{2} = 0\)

\[\underline{u} \cdot \underline{v} = |\underline{u}||\underline{v}|\cos\dfrac{\pi}{2}\]
\[\therefore\ \underline{u} \cdot \underline{v} = 0\]

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: As \(\underline{0} \cdot \underline{b} = 0\), for every vector \(\underline{b}\). So, the zero vector is regarded to be perpendicular to every vector.

(i) If \(\theta = 0\) or \(\pi\), the vectors \(\underline{u}\) and \(\underline{v}\) are collinear.
(ii) If \(\theta = \frac{\pi}{2}\), \(\cos\theta = 0 \Rightarrow \underline{u} \cdot \underline{v} = 0\)
So, the vectors \(\underline{u}\) and \(\underline{v}\) are perpendicular or orthogonal.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why this test is so useful: in space we cannot measure an angle with a protractor, but we can always compute a dot product from components. "If and only if" means it works both ways: perpendicular \(\Rightarrow\) dot product \(0\), and dot product \(0\) (for non-zero vectors) \(\Rightarrow\) perpendicular. "Orthogonal" is another word for perpendicular.
Corollary (i): when \(\theta = 0\) or \(\pi\) the vectors lie along one line; then \(\underline{u} \cdot \underline{v} = |\underline{u}||\underline{v}|\) or \(-|\underline{u}||\underline{v}|\).
Example of ours: \((\underline{i} + 2\underline{j} + 3\underline{k}) \cdot (4\underline{i} + \underline{j} - 2\underline{k}) = 4 + 2 - 6 = 0\), so these two vectors are perpendicular.

blocks.title: Example 9
steps:
Given: \(\underline{u} = 3\underline{i} - \underline{j} - 2\underline{k}\), \(\underline{v} = \underline{i} + 2\underline{j} - \underline{k}\).
To find: \(\underline{u} \cdot \underline{v}\).
Method: multiply matching components and add (14.2.5).

Step 1: Multiply matching components and add
\[\underline{u} \cdot \underline{v} = (3)(1) + (-1)(2) + (-2)(-1)\]
\[= 3 - 2 + 2 = 3\]
Why: \(\underline{u} \cdot \underline{v} = a_{1}a_{2} + b_{1}b_{2} + c_{1}c_{2}\); each product is written in brackets so that no sign is lost.

blocks.title: Example 10
blocks.problem: If \(\underline{u} = 2\underline{i} - 4\underline{j} + 5\underline{k}\) and \(\underline{v} = 4\underline{i} - 3\underline{j} - 4\underline{k}\), then prove that \(\underline{u}\) and \(\underline{v}\) are orthogonal.
steps:
Given: \(\underline{u} = 2\underline{i} - 4\underline{j} + 5\underline{k}\), \(\underline{v} = 4\underline{i} - 3\underline{j} - 4\underline{k}\).
To prove: \(\underline{u} \perp \underline{v}\).
Method: two non-zero vectors are orthogonal exactly when their dot product is \(0\); so compute \(\underline{u} \cdot \underline{v}\).

Step 1: Find the dot product
\[\underline{u} \cdot \underline{v} = (2)(4) + (-4)(-3) + (5)(-4)\]
\[= 8 + 12 - 20 = 0\]
Why: component formula of 14.2.5.

Step 2: Conclude
\[\underline{u} \cdot \underline{v} = 0 \Rightarrow \underline{u} \perp \underline{v}\]
Why: both vectors are non-zero, so a zero dot product means \(\cos\theta = 0\), i.e. \(\theta = \frac{\pi}{2}\).

Check:
Neither vector is zero: \(|\underline{u}| = \sqrt{45}\), \(|\underline{v}| = \sqrt{41}\). So the zero dot product really comes from the right angle.

blocks.title: Example 11
blocks.problem: Find a scalar \(\alpha\) so that the vectors \(2\underline{i} + \alpha\underline{j} + 5\underline{k}\) and \(3\underline{i} + \underline{j} + \alpha\underline{k}\) are orthogonal.
steps:
Given: \(\underline{u} = 2\underline{i} + \alpha\underline{j} + 5\underline{k}\), \(\underline{v} = 3\underline{i} + \underline{j} + \alpha\underline{k}\), orthogonal.
To find: \(\alpha\).
Method: orthogonal means \(\underline{u} \cdot \underline{v} = 0\); this gives an equation in \(\alpha\).

Step 1: Write the condition
\[\underline{u} \cdot \underline{v} = 0\]
\[(2\underline{i} + \alpha\underline{j} + 5\underline{k}) \cdot (3\underline{i} + \underline{j} + \alpha\underline{k}) = 0\]
Why: definition of orthogonal vectors.

Step 2: Expand
\[(2)(3) + (\alpha)(1) + (5)(\alpha) = 0\]
\[6 + \alpha + 5\alpha = 0\]
Why: matching components multiplied and added.

Step 3: Solve
\[6\alpha = -6 \Rightarrow \alpha = -1\]
Why: collect the \(\alpha\) terms and divide by \(6\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: In the book's Example 11 the line \(\Rightarrow (2\underline{i} + \alpha\underline{j} + 5\underline{k}) \cdot (3\underline{i} + \underline{j} + \alpha\underline{k})\) is printed without "\(= 0\)"; the equation is \((\dots) \cdot (\dots) = 0\), as written in our Step 1.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. Non-zero \(\underline{u} \perp \underline{v} \iff \underline{u} \cdot \underline{v} = 0\).
2. The zero vector counts as perpendicular to every vector.
3. To find an unknown that makes two vectors perpendicular, set the dot product equal to \(0\) and solve.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Sign errors in products such as \((-4)(-3) = 12\) and \((5)(-4) = -20\); one wrong sign hides the zero.
2. Setting the dot product equal to \(1\) instead of \(0\) for perpendicular vectors.
3. Treating parallel vectors as perpendicular: parallel vectors have \(\theta = 0\) or \(\pi\), not \(\frac{\pi}{2}\).
